lead: Social engineering is an attack on the person, not on the machine. The attacker does not break the cipher or the firewall. He calls the help desk, copies a bank's logo, and asks for one small favour until the password arrives. Phishing is the mass version of this, sent by mail, SMS or voice call. It exists because the cheapest way into a system is to be invited in by someone who has a valid login. It is used against bank and UPI customers, job seekers, students waiting for a scholarship, and staff of any organisation that has a mail server.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for threat, vulnerability and attack vector, because phishing is an attack vector that never touches the network.

blocks.text: Social engineering is any attack that makes a person, not a machine, give up a secret or break a rule. The attacker never solves the cipher. He becomes a trusted voice on the phone. Four levers do most of the work: authority (I am calling from the bank's security team), urgency (your account closes in 30 minutes), fear (a fraud has been detected in your name), and helpfulness or greed (claim your refund). Every good script pulls at least two of them at once.

items: Pretexting: the attacker invents a story and an identity, such as an IT engineer with a ticket number, an auditor, or a new joiner who lost the VPN password.
Baiting: something attractive is left where the victim will find it, such as a USB stick labelled Salary_2024 or a free download that asks for a login.
Tailgating: the attacker walks through a door behind a badge-holding employee, hands full, and never shows a badge.
Quid pro quo: a service is offered in return for cooperation, such as free IT support that needs the user to install a remote-access tool.

blocks.text: Only baiting needs technology, and that part is ordinary malware (1.5). The rest need a phone and confidence. That is why they survive every firewall upgrade.
Phishing is social engineering delivered as a message: mail, SMS or phone call. It is one-to-many, cheap, and measured in fractions of a rupee per target. The variants differ only in aim and channel.

head: Variant
Channel
What makes it different
rows: Researched; names the person's manager, project or travel plan
Aimed at senior staff who can approve payments
Short link hidden in a delivery, KYC or electricity-bill message
Live or recorded caller; the OTP is asked for aloud
Traffic redirected at DNS or the hosts file, so no click is needed
A copy of a real earlier mail with the link swapped for a fake one

blocks.text: Read the anatomy of a typical mail. The display name says ICICI Bank Alert, but the address ends in mail-secure.top. The domain is a lookalike: icici-bank-verify.com instead of icicibank.com. There is a deadline of a few hours. The button leads to a page with the real logo that asks for the net-banking password and then for the OTP. The OTP request is the giveaway: no bank asks for an OTP that it has just sent you.

Lookalike domains are built by typosquatting. The letters rn replace m (rnicrosoft), the digit 0 replaces the letter o, an extra hyphen is inserted, or .co replaces .com. Some use characters from another script, such as the Cyrillic a, which looks identical to the Latin a. Read a domain from the right: the word just before .com is the real owner, and everything to its left is chosen by the sender.
No single control stops phishing, so stack three.

items: People: short repeated training, a one-click report button in the mail client, and no blame when someone reports that they clicked. A reported mail protects everyone else in the company.

Mail: SPF lists the servers allowed to send for a domain. DKIM signs the message so tampering in transit is visible. DMARC tells the receiver what to do when SPF and DKIM both fail: none, quarantine or reject.
Technology: multi-factor authentication, a password manager that will not autofill on a lookalike domain, and link inspection by hovering before clicking or by opening the site from a saved bookmark.

blocks.where: E is the expected loss in rupees; N is the number of mails sent; p_click is the fraction of receivers who click the link; p_cred is the fraction of clickers who type a password; L is the average loss per taken account, in rupees.

blocks.text: Red-flag checklist. Any one item means stop and verify by a second channel, such as calling the number on the back of your card.

items: The greeting is generic, or your name is spelt wrongly.
The domain differs from the official one by a character, a hyphen or the suffix.
A deadline of hours, or a threat that the account will be closed or frozen.
The link opens a login page, or the mail asks for an OTP, PIN or CVV.
Bank details for a payment have changed, or the sender asks for secrecy.
You are asked to install something or to switch off a security setting.

spec.aria: Two funnels of chips side by side: 10,000 mails, 500 clicks, 50 passwords, 50 accounts and ₹20,00,000 lost; and 10,000 mails, 250 clicks, 25 passwords, 0 accounts and ₹0 lost.

examples.question: A phishing campaign sends 10,000 mails. 5% of receivers click the link, 10% of those who click type their password, and the average loss per taken account is ₹40,000. (a) Find the number of clicks. (b) Find the number of credentials captured. (c) Find the expected loss. (d) Training halves the click rate and multi-factor authentication blocks every password-only login. Find the loss from taken accounts after both changes.
steps: New click rate = 0.05 ÷ 2 = 0.025, so clicks = 0.025 × 10,000 = 250 clicks.
Multi-factor authentication rejects all 25 password-only logins, so taken accounts = 0.
New loss = 0 × ₹40,000 = ₹0. Only the training cost remains.
examples.answer: Expected loss falls from ₹20,00,000 to ₹0 once training halves the clicks and multi-factor authentication stops password-only logins.
examples.check:
mails = 10000
p_click = 0.05
p_cred = 0.10
L = 40000
clicks = p_click * mails
creds = p_cred * clicks
loss = creds * L
new_clicks = (p_click / 2) * mails
new_creds = p_cred * new_clicks
taken = 0
new_loss = taken * L
print(int(clicks))
print(int(creds))
print(int(loss))
print(int(new_clicks))
print(int(new_creds))
print(int(new_loss))

traps: Answering phishing with a mail filter alone. The marks are for the human layer: urgency, authority, a domain that differs from the real one, and a request for a password or OTP.
Mixing up pharming and phishing. Pharming needs no click; the address bar shows the correct name and the redirection happens at DNS or in the hosts file.
Mixing up smishing and vishing. Smishing is SMS, vishing is a voice call.
Claiming multi-factor authentication ends phishing. It stops password-only reuse, but a real-time proxy page or a forwarded OTP can still get through, so it is a backstop and not a cure.
Believing SPF, DKIM and DMARC prove a mail is honest. They only authenticate the sending domain; a freshly registered lookalike domain can pass all three.

quiz.q: Define social engineering and name the four levers it uses.
quiz.a: Social engineering is an attack that tricks a person into revealing a secret or breaking a rule. The levers are authority, urgency, fear, and helpfulness or greed.
Spear phishing aimed at senior staff such as directors or finance heads, who can approve large payments or release sensitive data.

quiz.q: Why does a password manager defend against a lookalike domain?
quiz.a: It matches the saved entry to the exact origin. On icici-bank-verify.com it finds no entry, so it stays silent instead of filling the password, and the user notices the missing autofill.

quiz.q: Give two differences between phishing and pharming.
quiz.a: Phishing arrives as a message and needs a click; pharming redirects traffic at DNS or the hosts file, so no message or click is needed. In phishing the wrong URL is visible in the link; in pharming the address bar shows the genuine name.

quiz.q: A campaign sends 20,000 mails. 4% click, 25% of clickers type a password, and the average loss per taken account is ₹25,000. Find the expected loss.
A lookalike domain passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Why, and what does this show about mail authentication?
quiz.a: The attacker owns that domain, so he publishes his own SPF and DKIM records and a DMARC policy for it. All three checks confirm that the mail came from that domain; they say nothing about whether the domain is the one the user thinks he is dealing with. Authentication is not trust.

quiz.q: A company has MFA on all accounts. Its staff still lose money to vishing. Explain how the attack skips the MFA control and suggest one fix.
quiz.a: In vishing the attacker persuades the user to read out the OTP or approve the push notification while he logs in with the stolen password on the real site. MFA verifies the login, not who is asking. Fixes: staff training that no one asks for an OTP, number matching on push prompts, and phishing-resistant hardware keys bound to the real origin.

beyond: Not for the exam. The industry direction is phishing-resistant login: passkeys and FIDO2 hardware keys are bound to the origin, so a fake page cannot use them even if the password leaks. On the detection side, mail gateways now score messages on header anomalies and on how new the sending domain is, not on keywords. Business email compromise, a thread hijack with no link at all, is the variant that defeats link scanners. Voice cloning makes vishing harder to spot by ear, which pushes verification back to a callback on a known number. Search for passkeys, WebAuthn, DMARC policy rollout and business email compromise.
